endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: Health system executive participants all stated that they would benefit from efforts to standardize metrics and adopt strategies to allow for cross-system comparisons. This would include agreed-upon metric definitions, aligned with domains of interest, and rigorous study design.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence documentation in trauma resuscitation: efficiency requires guardrails
endorsements.quote: The rate of errors should be measured and used to drive continuous improvement.

endorsements.title: Barriers and opportunities of scaling ambient AI scribes for clinical documentation across diverse healthcare settings
endorsements.quote: Health systems should consider including qualitative metrics that captures conciseness usability of documents, beyond simply time savings.

endorsements.title: Ambient AI Scribes as Emerging Infrastructure in the Learning Health System
endorsements.quote: Developing metrics for scribe‐mediated data quality will require defining what accurate documentation looks like in practice, likely through structured clinician review against source audio, patient‐reported accuracy under open notes frameworks, and comparison against established documentation standards such as those used in medical audits.

evidence.title: Clinician-Centered Evaluation of Large Language Model-Generated Discharge Summaries for Longer Hospitalizations: Insights from Hospitalists and Primary Care Physicians
evidence.outcome: Annotated errors (omissions, hallucinations) in LLM vs human discharge summaries, rated by clinicians
evidence.effect: LLM-generated summaries had fewer annotated errors, primarily due to fewer omissions, without increased estimated harm potential or likelihood versus human-authored summaries.
evidence.quote: LLM-generated summaries had fewer annotated errors, primarily due to fewer omissions, without increased estimated harm potential or likelihood compared with human-authored summaries.

evidence.title: Are automated documentation-error judges fit to measure ambient AI scribes? A pre-registered, blinded human-validation study
evidence.outcome: Validity of automated judges detecting scribe note errors versus blinded clinician adjudication
evidence.effect: Judge-clinician agreement 64% (95% CI 60 to 68); inter-clinician AC1 0.24; concordance on 77 consensus items 70% (95% CI 59 to 79); genuine-error rate among flagged 68% (94% CrI 48 to 83).
evidence.quote: On 77 consensus items the pipeline concurred on 70% (95% CI 59 to 79).
evidence.sample_unit: pipeline-flagged documentation items (565 adjudications by 10 clinicians)

evidence.title: Using ChatGPT-4 to Create Structured Medical Notes From Audio Recordings of Physician-Patient Encounters: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Errors in AI-generated SOAP notes: omissions, additions, incorrect facts versus gold standard
evidence.effect: 23.6 errors per clinical case on average; omissions 86%, additions 10.5%, incorrect facts 3.2%.
evidence.quote: Although ChatGPT-4 consistently generated SOAP-style notes, there were, on average, 23.6 errors per clinical case, with errors of omission (86%) being the most common, followed by addition errors (10.5%) and inclusion of incorrect facts (3.2%).

evidence.title: Use of large language models to optimize poison center charting
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated appropriateness of LLM summaries and accuracy of tabulated data points
evidence.effect: 80% of summaries had median score high enough to be appropriate for entry into the medical record; 91% of data points correctly abstracted into table format.
evidence.quote: Eighty percent of summaries had a median score high enough to be deemed appropriate for entry into the medical record.

evidence.title: A framework to assess clinical safety and hallucination rates of LLMs for medical text summarisation
evidence.outcome: Hallucination and omission rates in LLM-generated notes across 18 experiments, clinician-annotated by severity
evidence.effect: Of 12,999 sentences, 191 had hallucinations (1.47%), 84 (44%) major; 1712 of 49,590 transcript sentences omitted (3.45%), 286 (16.7%) major. Iterative refinement cut major omissions from 61 to 0.
evidence.quote: Of 12,999 sentences in 450 clinical notes, 191 sentences had hallucinations (1.47%), of which 84 sentences (44%) were major (could impact patient diagnosis and management if left uncorrected).

evidence.title: Vision-Enabled AI scribes reduce omissions in clinical conversations: evidence from simulated medication histories
evidence.outcome: Ambient scribe documentation accuracy and omission errors, video input vs audio-only
evidence.effect: Vision-enabled scribe achieved 98% accuracy (2114/2,160 data points); video outperformed audio-only (98% vs 81%, P < 0.001), mainly via fewer omissions (10 vs 358 errors).
evidence.quote: Video input significantly outperformed audio-only processing (98% vs 81%, P < 0.001), primarily through reduced omissions (10 vs 358 errors).
evidence.sample_unit: simulated medication history test recordings (2160 data points)

evidence.title: MedFactEval and MedAgentBrief: A Framework and Workflow for Generating and Evaluating Factual Clinical Summaries
evidence.venue: Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing. Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM Jury with seven-physician majority vote on key-fact inclusion in generated summaries
evidence.effect: LLM Jury achieved Cohen's κ = 81% with the physician panel, statistically non-inferior to a single human expert (κ = 67%, P < 0.001).
evidence.quote: The MedFactEval LLM Jury achieved almost perfect agreement with this panel (Cohen's κ = 81%), a performance statistically non-inferior to that of a single human expert (κ = 67%, P < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: inpatient cases with clinician-defined key facts

evidence.title: Responsible AI for Personalized Patient Education and Engagement Across Medical Conditions: Leveraging Multi-Agent LLMs, Ambient Technology, and NotebookLM-A Case Study in Diabetes Education and Limb Preservation
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association
evidence.outcome: Expert evaluation of ambient scribe SOAP notes and summaries for hallucinations, accuracy, completeness
evidence.effect: Three outcomes passed validation criteria including accuracy, completeness, comprehensiveness, absence of potential harm, and no hallucination; no hallucinations were found.
evidence.quote: Three outcomes successfully passed the validation criteria, including accuracy, completeness, comprehensiveness, absence of potential harm, and no hallucination.
evidence.sample_unit: simulated consultations and pre-recorded training videos

evidence.title: AI-Assisted Clinical Data Abstraction From Electronic Health Records: Retrospective Concordance Study
evidence.outcome: AI extraction concordance with human abstraction; spurious values and omissions
evidence.effect: Exact match 92% for NRS (95% CI 84-96; ICC=0.96) and 94% for VPS (95% CI 84-98; κ=0.91); all discrepancies minor, no spurious values generated.
evidence.quote: All discrepancies were minor, and no spurious values were generated.

evidence.title: Accuracy of Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model-Generated Preconsult Summaries in Breast Surgical Oncology
evidence.outcome: Field-level accuracy, omission, and fabrication of LLM-generated summaries versus staff-authored summaries
evidence.effect: Fabrication ≤2% per field; nodal status accuracy 95% v 72%, invasive tumor on biopsy 94% v 30%; staff more accurate for receptor status 96% v 86%; patient-level fabrication 8% AI vs 3% staff.
evidence.quote: At the patient level, fabrication occurred in 16 AI-generated summaries (8%), including six clinically significant cases (3%).

evidence.title: VozConsultAI: A Provider-Agnostic Architecture and a Clinically Grounded Evaluation of Open-Weight Large Language Models for SOAP Note Extraction in Brazilian Portuguese Telehealth
evidence.outcome: SOAP note quality including hallucination penalty across five open-weight LLMs
evidence.effect: DeepSeek V3.2 achieved the best consolidated quality (0.87) and the highest clinical grounding (0.96); assessment and plan sections account for most errors.
evidence.quote: DeepSeek V3.2 achieved the best consolidated quality (0.87) and the highest clinical grounding (0.96).

evidence.title: Beyond word error rate: clinical risk as the necessary standard for ambient AI scribe evaluation: evidence from 77 global languages
evidence.outcome: Whether frequency metrics like WER track clinically consequential scribe transcription errors
evidence.effect: None of six frequency metrics showed detectable association with serious clinical risk (|Spearman ρ|<0.16); 251 (0.42%) of 59,819 errors CRITICAL/HIGH; clinical-risk assessment complements WER.
evidence.quote: None of six frequency metrics showed a statistically detectable association with serious clinical risk across languages; correlations were small (absolute Spearman ρ<0.16).
languages: 77 languages (translated from 99), including high-resource and low-resource languages

evidence.title: A Randomized-Clinical Trial of Two Ambient Artificial Intelligence Scribes: Measuring Documentation Efficiency and Physician Burnout
evidence.outcome: Physician-reported clinically significant inaccuracies in scribe-generated notes
evidence.effect: Clinically significant inaccuracies noted 'occasionally' (Likert DAX 2.7 vs Nabla 2.8; p=.68). One Grade 1 adverse event was reported.
evidence.quote: One Grade 1 (mild) adverse event was reported, while clinically-significant inaccuracies were noted “occasionally” on 5-point Likert questions (DAX 2.7 [2.4-3.0] vs. Nabla 2.8 [2.6-3.0]; p=.68).

evidence.title: Ambient AI Scribes in Clinical Practice: A Randomized Trial
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported clinically significant inaccuracies in ambient scribe notes
evidence.effect: Clinically significant inaccuracies noted 'occasionally' on five-point Likert questions (DAX 2.7 [95% CI 2.4 to 3.0]; Nabla 2.8 [95% CI 2.6 to 3.0]).
evidence.quote: One grade 1 (mild) adverse event was reported, while clinically significant inaccuracies were noted "occasionally" on five-point Likert questions (DAX 2.7 [95% CI, 2.4 to 3.0]; Nabla 2.8 [95% CI, 2.6 to 3.0]).

evidence.title: Evaluating the Impact of Artificial Intelligence Scribes on Clinical Workflow and Documentation Quality: A Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.outcome: Medical errors in AI scribe versus conventional documentation, reviewed by the surgeon
evidence.effect: 19 medical errors in the AI scribe group vs 9 in the conventional group; no significant difference in spelling or grammatical errors.
evidence.quote: There were 19 medical errors in the AI scribe group compared to only nine errors in the conventional group.

evidence.title: Ambient AI Scribes to Create Educational Feedback Notes for Medical Students: Randomized Trial
evidence.outcome: Factual accuracy of unedited AI feedback summaries: mischaracterization and hallucination rates
evidence.effect: Of 117 AI-generated feedback elements, 6.8% (n=8) were mischaracterized and 1.7% (n=2) were hallucinated.
evidence.quote: Review of 117 AI-generated feedback elements showed a 6.8% (n=8) mischaracterization and 1.7% (n=2) hallucination rate, with most errors corrected during editing.

evidence.title: A Novel Playbook for Pragmatic Trial Operations to Monitor and Evaluate Ambient Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice
evidence.outcome: ICD-10 documentation accuracy following a note template change
evidence.effect: Documentation accuracy decreased from 79% (95% CI, 72 to 86%) to 35% (95% CI, 28 to 42%) following a note template change.
evidence.quote: A brief workflow issue related to a note template change initially reduced ICD-10 documentation accuracy from 79% (95% confidence interval [CI], 72 to 86%) to 35% (95% CI, 28 to 42%); accuracy returned to baseline after note template redesign and user training.

evidence.title: Ambient Artificial Intelligence Versus Human Scribes in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Blinded physician-rated quality of ambient scribe notes using PDQI-9 compared with human scribe notes
evidence.effect: Adult note quality similar; pediatric AI notes scored lower (41.36 vs 42.25, aRR -1.89 [95% CI -3.58 to -0.20]).
evidence.quote: PDQI-9 scores were similar for adults, but AI scribes scored lower for pediatric patients (41.36 versus 42.25, adjusted risk ratio [aRR] = -1.89 [95% confidence interval (CI) -3.58 to -0.20]).

evidence.title: Evaluating Patient and Professional Satisfaction and Documentation Time Reduction Through AI-Driven Automatic Clinical Note Generation in Primary Care: Proof-of-Concept Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported errors in AI-generated consultation notes, including hallucinations, and edit burden
evidence.effect: Context or meaning errors were most frequent; unsupported additions or hallucinations were uncommon; 26% of drafts required no edits; most reviews were <24 corrected words per minute.
evidence.quote: A qualitative analysis of clinician feedback showed that context or meaning errors were the most frequent, while unsupported additions or hallucinations were uncommon.

evidence.title: Reporting efficiency in diagnostic imaging: Can plug-and-play general-purpose large language models outperform conventional speech recognition?
evidence.outcome: Errors in LLM-generated radiology reports including confabulations, rewording, non-compliance
evidence.effect: In the LLM group: 69 instances of rewording without loss of meaning, 99 instances of non-compliance to instructions and 4 confabulations; grammar/spelling and transcription errors were fewer than CSR (79 vs 293; 225 vs 445).
evidence.quote: In the LLM group, 69 instances of rewording without loss of meaning, 99 instances of non-compliance to instructions and 4 confabulations were observed.

evidence.title: Implementing AI‑Powered Ambient Listening in Medication Reviews: Study Protocol and Pilot Evaluation in Belgian Community Pharmacies
evidence.outcome: Completeness of ambient scribe transcripts and summaries, including medication name recognition
evidence.effect: Incomplete recognition of medication names and dialect/accent issues produced incomplete transcripts and summaries; no quantitative accuracy reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Current challenges include the comprehensive recognition of medication names and uneven performance with certain regional dialects and/or accents, which can lead to incomplete transcripts and summaries.

evidence.title: Clinician Experiences with Ambient AI Scribe Technology in Singapore: A Qualitative Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported accuracy concerns and hallucinations in ambient scribe notes
evidence.effect: Clinicians reported accuracy concerns and AI hallucinations as persistent barriers; no error rates quantified.
evidence.quote: Persistent barriers included accuracy concerns, AI hallucinations, limited multilingual functionality, loss of documentation style, and uncertainties around compliance with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA).

evidence.title: Clinician Perspectives on an Ambient AI Scribe in the Emergency Department: A Cross-Sectional Pilot Survey
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported accuracy limitations of ambient scribe notes in the ED
evidence.effect: Accuracy limitations were a recurring concern in 10/34 responses, while 32/34 (94%) reported enhanced documentation quality. Accuracy was not measured against a reference standard.
evidence.quote: Content analysis identified documentation efficiency (21/34) and note detail capture (21/34) as the most emphasized strengths, with accuracy limitations (10/34) and workflow friction (6/34) as recurring concerns.
evidence.sample_unit: clinicians (34 survey responses across two rounds)

evidence.title: AI-driven simplification of surgical reports in gynecologic oncology: A potential tool for patient education
evidence.outcome: Clinical expert rating of accuracy and medical precision of AI-simplified reports
evidence.effect: Clinical experts raised concerns about lack of medical precision in the simplified reports despite better accessibility.
evidence.quote: However, despite the reports being more accessible and relevant, clinical experts highlighted concerns about their lack of medical precision.

evidence.title: Clinicians' rationale for editing ambient AI-drafted clinical notes: persistent challenges and implications for improvement
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported reasons for editing ambient AI drafts (transcription, attribution, omission errors)
evidence.effect: Clinicians edited drafts because of transcription errors, speaker attribution mistakes, overconfident unsupported statements, missing key clinical details, and lack of patient context. No numeric rates reported.
evidence.quote: Such editing was necessary due to reasons such as transcription errors, speaker attribution mistakes, overconfident statements without evidence, missing key clinical details, and AI's lack of information about the patient context.

evidence.title: What do clinicians edit in ambient AI-drafted clinical documentation? A qualitative content analysis
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Frequency of clinician edits to ambient AI note content (facts, orders, symptoms, medications, diagnoses)
evidence.effect: Most edited content was clinical facts: orders 40.0%, symptoms 30.3%, medication prescriptions 27.3%, diagnosis descriptions 25.9%; terminology edits 11.6%, language style 7.2%.
evidence.quote: The most frequently edited content pertained to clinical facts including orders (eg, procedures, lab tests) (40.0%), symptoms (30.3%), medication prescriptions (27.3%), and diagnosis descriptions (25.9%).

evidence.title: Voice-Based Structured Nursing Documentation Using Automatic Speech Recognition and Large Language Models: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Hallucination rate in LLM-generated DART notes from ASR transcripts
evidence.effect: Hallucination rate was 2.51%; DART generation macro F1 0.82 (95% CI 0.80-0.84).
evidence.quote: The hallucination rate was 2.51%.

evidence.title: Implementation of an AI-Assisted Workflow for Rehabilitation Discharge Summary Creation: Evaluation of Documentation Efficiency, Usability, and Hallucinations in a 290-Bed General Hospital in Japan
evidence.outcome: Hallucinations and omissions in AI-generated rehabilitation discharge summaries rated by two raters
evidence.effect: 9 of 11 summaries (81.8%) contained at least one error; 19 hallucinations and 1 omission; major errors 52.6% (10/19); fabrication-type hallucinations major rate 83.3% (5/6).
evidence.quote: In the hallucination and omission evaluation, 9 of 11 rehabilitation discharge summaries (81.8%) contained at least one error, yielding a total of 19 hallucinations and 1 omission.
evidence.sample_unit: post-implementation rehabilitation discharge summaries (documentation time); 18 therapists for SUS; 11 summaries for hallucination review

evidence.title: An Evaluation of AI-Generated Clinical Notes in the OpenNotes Era: A Thematic Analysis of Clinician Discourse
evidence.venue: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
evidence.outcome: Clinician perceptions of hallucinations in AI-generated notes
evidence.effect: Clinicians framed AI hallucinations as a mathematically inevitable epistemic risk rather than a correctable technical bug (qualitative theme, no rates reported).
evidence.quote: Second, clinicians frame AI hallucinations as a mathematically inevitable epistemic risk rather than a correctable technical bug.
evidence.sample_unit: Reddit comments (120 threads, eight clinician subreddits)

evidence.title: Ambient AI in primary care: an exploratory mixed methods survey of UK general practitioners
evidence.outcome: GP-reported frequency and severity of errors in ambient scribe notes
evidence.effect: 32% (n=45) reported errors often/always, including 14% (n=20) with significant-to-critical implications.
evidence.quote: Errors were common but usually minor: 32% (n=45) reported errors often/always, including 14% (n=20) with significant-to-critical implications.
evidence.sample_unit: GP users of ambient AI scribes (of 1003 survey respondents)

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Electronic Medical Record Summarization in Breast Surgical Oncology
evidence.outcome: Omissions and errors in AI-generated outside-record summaries rated by clinicians
evidence.effect: Thoroughness without omission rated low in 28 (45%) of 62 summaries; errors in 25 (40%) surveys, 13 (52%) treatment-impacting; imaging errors most common (17, 68%).
evidence.quote: Thoroughness without omission was rated low in 28 (45%) summaries.

evidence.title: Deployment of an ambient AI scribe in emergency care: A 12-month evaluation in a large Spanish hospital network
evidence.outcome: Transcription accuracy and audited documentation quality of scribe-generated emergency reports
evidence.effect: Mean transcription accuracy 93.9% and stable over 12 months; audited quality scores higher for Scribe-generated reports with a large effect size.
evidence.quote: Transcription accuracy remained high and stable throughout the study (mean: 93.9 %).

evidence.title: Evaluation of Socio-Technical Mechanisms Shaping AI Scribe Documentation Failures: A Netnographic Study
evidence.venue: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported AI scribe note problems such as misattribution, hallucinations, omissions
evidence.effect: Clinicians reported content problems including misattribution, hallucinations and omissions, plus workflow disruptions such as latency, crashes and copy-and-paste friction. No frequency rates given.
evidence.quote: Reported problems included content-related issues, such as misattribution, hallucinations and omissions, as well as workflow disruptions, including latency, crashes and copy-and-paste friction.
evidence.sample_unit: data segments (from 952 documents across 162 Reddit threads)

evidence.title: Assessing Large Language Model Utility and Limitations in Diabetes Education: A Cross-Sectional Study of Patient Interactions and Specialist Evaluations
evidence.outcome: Specialist-rated accuracy and hallucinations in ChatGPT answers to patient diabetes questions
evidence.effect: Reviewers detected occasional inaccuracies and hallucinations; 98% of answers judged informative and empathetic; ophthalmologists rated clarity 3.09/5 and completeness 2.94/5.
evidence.quote: Reviewers detected occasional inaccuracies and hallucinations.

evidence.title: Ambient Only vs. Longitudinal Data-Enhanced AI Documentation: A Pilot Study Quantifying the Value of Historical Clinical Context in Primary Care
evidence.outcome: Ambient documentation completeness
evidence.effect: Completeness domain improvement with history was 42.5 points; P<0.001.
evidence.quote: The largest improvements was observed in the completeness domain (difference 42.5 points; P<0.001).

evidence.title: Quality and Safety profiles of AI-Generated vs Clinician-Generated Handoffs in Hospital Medicine
evidence.outcome: Hallucinations, inaccuracies, and omissions in AI-generated handoffs versus clinician-authored handoffs
evidence.effect: Error rates comparable (0.3/handoff both groups); AI errors included inaccuracies (9%) and hallucinations (1%), while clinician handoffs contained only omissions; AI accuracy lower (4.1 vs 4.4, p=0.03).
evidence.quote: Error rates were comparable (0.3/handoff in both groups); however, AI-generated handoffs included inaccuracies (9% of AI errors) and hallucinations (1% of AI errors), while clinician-authored handoffs contained only omissions.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Assessment of Psychosis Risk
evidence.outcome: Faithfulness of generated summaries and clinically relevant confabulation rate
evidence.effect: Summaries largely faithful to source transcripts, with low rates of clinically relevant confabulation (3%).
evidence.quote: Generated summaries were largely faithful to source transcripts, with low rates of clinically relevant confabulation (3%).
evidence.country: Multi-country (research sites; not specified in text)

evidence.title: Quality, consistency, and clinical safety of AI-generated versus clinician-written clinical notes: a multi-country paired simulation study
evidence.outcome: Proportion of notes with at least one Critical+High documentation error, AI vs clinician notes
evidence.effect: AI notes had fewer Critical+High errors: 24.4% vs 61.0% (calibrated reviewer; RR 2.50) and 6.2% vs 21.8% (clinician adjudication; RR 3.50). Nonzero AI error burden remained; difference largest for omissions.
evidence.quote: On the principal safety outcome — the paired probability that a note carried ≥1 Critical+High error — clinician notes were affected more often under both detection arms: 61.0% versus 24.4% by the calibrated reviewer (relative risk 2.50, 95% CI 2.09–3.00) and 21.8% versus 6.2% by clinician adjudication (relative risk 3.50, 95% CI 2.32–5.27).
evidence.country: United Kingdom, Spain, Italy, France, Germany

evidence.title: Evaluating LLMs for HIV Epidemiological Surveillance in Spanish: Clinical Summarization, Risk Factor Extraction, and Inference Stability across Models
evidence.outcome: Physician-rated harm severity of hallucinations, omissions, inaccuracies in LLM clinical summaries
evidence.effect: Gemini flash had lower severity scores than GPT open-weight across all error categories; hallucinations rare in best model (mean score 0.04) but not absent.
evidence.quote: Hallucinations were rare in the best-performing model (mean score 0.04), although not entirely absent.

evidence.title: Does a Safety-Priming Instruction Reduce Risk-Fact Omission in Psychiatric Note Summarization? A Synthetic-Vignette Study of Small Open-Weight Language Models
evidence.outcome: Omission of embedded safety-critical risk fact in LLM psychiatric note summaries under generic prompt
evidence.effect: Baseline risk-fact omission ranged from 4% to 26% across four models; smallest model omitted the risk fact about one time in four; suicidality omitted up to 50% for weaker models.
evidence.quote: Baseline (generic-instruction) risk-fact omission ranges from 4% to 26% across the four models the smallest model omits the safety-critical fact roughly one time in four.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic psychiatric intake vignettes per condition

evidence.title: Mind the gap: emergent clinical risk at the interface of two individually safe AI systems in a multilingual ambient scribe
evidence.outcome: Serious errors, including ASR-derived and note-originated, in ambient scribe notes
evidence.effect: Intrinsic serious-error rate 3.4%; of serious in-note errors in end-to-end, 87% ASR-derived and 7% note-originated; amplification exceeded correction threefold.
evidence.quote: Of serious in-note errors, 87% were ASR-derived and 7% note-originated; amplification exceeded correction threefold (fate entropy 1.19 bits).
evidence.sample_unit: scripted consultation sessions (end-to-end arm; 385 in intrinsic arm)
languages: 77 languages including high-, medium-, and low-resource languages

evidence.title: The Impact of Acoustic and Informational Noise on AI-Generated Clinical Summaries
evidence.outcome: Scribe note omissions, hallucinations and inclusions relative to ground-truth summary
evidence.effect: Omissions were the principal error; at 4.5 m all facts omitted; up to 2 m only <5 omissions for all microphones except laptop.
evidence.quote: At 4.5 m from the consultation, for all microphones tested, all facts were omitted.

evidence.title: Transcribing multilingual radiologist-patient dialogue into mammography reports using AI: A step towards patient-centric radiology
evidence.outcome: Errors in AI-generated mammography reports (missed/incorrect information)
evidence.effect: Errors present in 50% of AI-generated reports, predominantly missed and incorrect information, with higher error rate in malignant cases; mean concordance 0.94.
evidence.quote: Errors were present in 50% of AI-generated reports, predominantly missed and incorrect information, with a higher error rate in malignant cases.

evidence.title: Validation of a Deep Learning Chest X-ray Interpretation Model: Integrating Large-Scale AI and Large Language Models for Comparative Analysis with ChatGPT
evidence.outcome: Hallucination rate in AI chest X-ray readings rated by two radiologists
evidence.effect: KARA-CXR non-hallucination rate 75% vs ChatGPT 38%; hallucinations frequent, especially in ChatGPT. Interobserver agreement 0.91 (KARA) and 0.85 (GPT4).
evidence.quote: KARA-CXR demonstrated a non-hallucination rate of 75%, which is significantly higher than ChatGPT's 38%.

evidence.title: From jargon to clarity: Improving the readability of foot and ankle radiology reports with an artificial intelligence large language model
evidence.venue: Foot and ankle surgery : official journal of the European Society of Foot and Ankle Surgeons
evidence.outcome: Hallucination rate in AI-generated patient-facing radiology explanations
evidence.effect: Hallucination rates were 4% (X-ray), 7% (CT), and 6% (MRI); mean Likert accuracy scores were 4.0, 3.9, and 3.9 out of 5.
evidence.quote: The rate of hallucinations in the AI-LLM generated X-Ray report, CT report and MRI report was 4%, 7% and 6%, respectively.

evidence.title: ChatGPT-4 generates orthopedic discharge documents faster than humans maintaining comparable quality: a pilot study of 6 cases
evidence.outcome: Hallucination events in AI-generated discharge documents versus physician-written
evidence.effect: 4 hallucination events found in ChatGPT-4-generated content, compared with 6 events in physician-produced notes; quality comparable overall.
evidence.quote: 4 events of hallucinations were found in the ChatGPT-4-generated content, compared with 6 events in the human/physician produced notes.
evidence.sample_unit: fictional orthopedic cases (discharge documents rated by 15 expert panelists)

evidence.title: A pilot feasibility study comparing large language models in extracting key information from ICU patient text records from an Irish population
evidence.outcome: LLM ICU summary capture of key clinical events and hallucinations, adjudicated by intensivists
evidence.effect: Key event identification was 41.5 ± 15.2% for GPT-4 API, 19.2 ± 20.9% for ChatGPT and 16.5 ± 14.1% for Llama2 (p = 0.002). GPT-4 API produced minor hallucinations.
evidence.quote: Overall ability to identify a pre-defined list of important clinical events in the summary was 41.5 ± 15.2% for GPT-4 API, 19.2 ± 20.9% for ChatGPT and 16.5 ± 14.1% for Llama2 (p = 0.002).
evidence.sample_unit: ICU episodes (one summary per LLM per episode)

evidence.title: Large language models can support generation of standardized discharge summaries - A retrospective study utilizing ChatGPT-4 and electronic health records
evidence.outcome: Hallucinations and content mistakes in AI-generated discharge summaries rated by blinded specialists
evidence.effect: Hallucinations present in 40% of AI-DS, 37.5% deemed highly clinically relevant; minor content mistakes in 30% of AI vs 10% of human DS.
evidence.quote: Hallucinations were present in 40 % of AI-DS, with 37.5 % deemed highly clinically relevant.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence as a modality to enhance the readability of neurosurgical literature for patients
evidence.outcome: Physician-rated scientific accuracy of AI-generated layperson summaries
evidence.effect: 68.4% of GPT3.5 and 84.2% of GPT4 summaries maintained moderate scientific accuracy per two physician reviewers, so a substantial share did not.
evidence.quote: A total of 68.4% and 84.2% of GPT3.5- and GPT4-generated summaries, respectively, maintained moderate scientific accuracy according to the two physician-reviewers.

evidence.title: Evaluation Framework of Large Language Models in Medical Documentation: Development and Usability Study
evidence.outcome: Error types and counts in LLM-generated ED records, and correlation with clinical scores
evidence.effect: Invalid generation errors most common (35.38% of errors); structural malformation had largest negative impact on clinical score (r=-0.654); error count correlated with lower scores (r=-0.633).
evidence.quote: Quantitative analysis revealed that invalid generation errors were the most common, constituting 35.38% of total errors, while structural malformation errors had the most significant negative impact on the clinical evaluation score (Pearson r=-0.654; P<.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Models in extracting cognitive exam dates and scores
evidence.outcome: LLM extraction errors including hallucinations and wrong-test or wrong-date reports in clinical notes
evidence.effect: MMSE: LlaMA-2 had 27 total hallucinations, 19 wrong-test, 25 missed scores, 23 wrong dates; ChatGPT had 3 hallucinations, 17 wrong-test, 19 wrong dates.
evidence.quote: LlaMA-2 errors included 27 cases of total hallucination, 19 cases of reporting other scores instead of MMSE, 25 missed scores, and 23 cases of reporting only the wrong date.

evidence.title: Translating ophthalmic medical jargon with artificial intelligence: a comparative comprehension study
evidence.venue: Canadian journal of ophthalmology. Journal canadien d'ophtalmologie
evidence.outcome: Translation errors identified by ophthalmologist raters in LLM-translated notes
evidence.effect: All models exhibited some translation errors; ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-4.0 had fewer inaccuracies.
evidence.quote: All models exhibited some translation errors, but ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-4.0 had fewer inaccuracies.

evidence.title: Comparative Analysis of M4CXR, an LLM-Based Chest X-Ray Report Generation Model, and ChatGPT in Radiological Interpretation
evidence.outcome: Hallucination and false findings in AI-generated chest X-ray reports rated by radiologists
evidence.effect: M4CXR showed fewer hallucinations than ChatGPT; diagnostic acceptability was about 60-62% for M4CXR versus 42-45% for ChatGPT, so many reports were unacceptable.
evidence.quote: For diagnostic accuracy, M4CXR achieved approximately 60-62% acceptability ratings compared to ChatGPT's 42-45%.

evidence.title: Development of a Preliminary Patient Safety Classification System for Generative AI
evidence.outcome: Errors in ambient digital scribe notes, categorised by type and clinical significance
evidence.effect: 66 errors across 11 simulated patient visits; omission most common (83% of errors); 55% low and 45% moderate clinical significance.
evidence.quote: Similarly, in the ADS simulation, we identified 66 errors across 11 patient visits, with omission being the most common (83% of errors).

commentary.bottom_line: Twelve offline or benchmark studies show that hallucination, omission, and term-recall metrics can be applied to AI-generated notes, but rater agreement is inconsistent and no study tested whether a health system evaluation program reduces errors that reach patients. No testing study measured speaker misattribution or coding accuracy.

perspectives.view: All 12 studies that test the practice are level 4 or 5 and use offline replays, simulated encounters, or automated benchmarks. They show that defined metrics can be applied and produce error rates. None measured whether a health system's evaluation program reduces errors in signed notes or harm to patients. Indirectness and inconsistent rater agreement lower certainty.

In 450 UK transcript-note pairs, 1.47% of note sentences contained hallucinations, 44% of them major, and 3.45% of transcript sentences were omitted. Iterative refinement cut major omissions from 61 to 0. Across 59,819 transcription errors, no frequency metric tracked serious clinical risk (|ρ|<0.16), which suggests severity grading may be needed beyond word error rate.

Rater agreement varied across studies. Ten clinicians adjudicating 434 flagged items reached an inter-clinician AC1 of 0.24, and an automated judge agreed with clinicians 64% of the time. An LLM jury reached κ of 81% against a seven-physician panel, compared with 67% for a single expert. A vision-enabled scribe recorded 98% medication data accuracy in simulation.

Health system executives in the guidance source asked for shared metric definitions so that systems can compare results. Clinician adjudication takes staff time, and one study used 10 clinicians for 565 adjudications. Automated judges could lower that cost, but agreement of 64% in one study and κ of 81% in another suggests local validation may be needed before they replace clinician review.

Two testing studies involved non-English or limited English proficiency material, and both were benchmark-only. One used 30 synthetic Brazilian teleconsultations, and the other used a UK transcription-error set. A Belgian hazard study reported that dialect and accent problems produced incomplete transcripts, which suggests quality metrics may perform differently for these speakers.

One endorsing commentary proposes patient-reported accuracy under open notes as a quality measure, but no testing study asked patients to review their notes. In 200 breast oncology consultations, patient-level fabrication was 8% for AI summaries versus 3% for staff summaries. This suggests patients may benefit from a way to flag errors in their records.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared live deployments with and without a structured note-evaluation program on errors in signed notes, downstream diagnosis documentation, coding accuracy, or patient harm. Validated and reliable metrics for speaker misattribution and coding accuracy are absent, and inter-rater agreement standards for clinician and automated judges have not been established.
commentary.underserved_note: Two testing studies included non-English or limited English proficiency material, and both were benchmark-only studies without real patients. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that published error rates or metric validity carry over to accented speech, interpreted visits, or low-literacy encounters without local evaluation.
